extracted.intended_audience: authors of systematic reviews and meta-analyses (health/medical research)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, conducting, and reporting systematic reviews and meta-analyses, including which outcomes and effect measures to pre-specify, analytic methods, risk-of-bias assessments, and presentation of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-specify primary outcomes and summary effect measures
rubrics_metrics.description: When planning a systematic review, it is generally desirable that authors pre-specify the outcomes of primary interest (see Item 5) as well as the intended summary effect measure for each outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chosen summary effect measure may differ from that used in some included studies; if possible explain choice of effect measures though it may be hard to judge in advance which is most appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of summary measures for binary, continuous, and time-to-event outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: For binary outcomes common summary measures are risk ratio, odds ratio, and risk difference; for continuous outcomes the natural effect measure is difference in means (or standardized difference in means when scales differ); for time-to-event outcomes the hazard ratio is most common and reviewers need the log hazard ratio and its standard error for meta-analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relative effects (e.g., risk ratios) are more consistent across studies than absolute effects, but absolute differences are important for interpretation. Standardized mean differences are used when studies measure the same outcome on different scales. Risk/odds ratios for events by a fixed time are not equivalent to hazard ratios; median survival times are not a reliable basis for meta-analysis. If authors used different measures, describe methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planned methods of analysis (Item 14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the methods of handling data and combining results of studies, including measures of consistency (e.g., I2) for each meta-analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report any data transformations or processing (combining groups, aligning scales, reconstructing or imputing SDs, converting time-to-event data). If meta-analysis is done, specify the effect measure (see Item 13), the statistical method (e.g., inverse variance), and whether a fixed- or random-effects approach or alternative (e.g., Bayesian) was used; explain reasons for those choices. Report how between-study variability (heterogeneity/inconsistency) will be evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report details of data processing and imputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Report details of any data transformation or processing needed before analysis or presentation (e.g., combining intervention groups, aligning scale directions, reconstructing standard deviations, approximating within-patient variance, converting time-to-event data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how imputations were done (e.g., imputing SD from mean of known SDs), note which results were estimated rather than directly reported, and which items had missing information that could not be obtained. Contact original investigators when possible; if information is imputed, say how and for which items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deciding whether to combine data (Box 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision to combine study results statistically should consider statistical, clinical, and methodological factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clinical considerations depend on the review question (broad questions may allow combining more disparate studies). Methodological considerations include excluding low- and high-risk-of-bias studies from combination. There may be no single right choice; be transparent and describe key decisions to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-analysis model and methods, and assessment of consistency (Box 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If combining results statistically, choose appropriate meta-analysis model and method (fixed-effect vs random-effects; methods such as Mantel-Haenszel, inverse variance, DerSimonian-Laird, or Bayesian). Assess consistency/heterogeneity (Cochran's Q, I2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain differences: fixed-effect assumes common treatment effect and considers within-study variability only; random-effects assumes study effects vary and accounts for between-study variability. Random-effects gives more weight to small trials. Use I2 to quantify percentage of variation due to heterogeneity and report uncertainty for I2 (e.g., 95% CI). Be cautious interpreting heterogeneity when few studies are available. Consider reasons for heterogeneity and beware of data extraction errors as a cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify assessments of risk of bias across studies (Item 15)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify any assessment of risk of bias that may affect the cumulative evidence (e.g., publication bias, selective reporting within studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate missing studies and selective reporting using graphical (funnel plots) and formal statistical tests (Egger's test, adjusted rank correlation, regression asymmetry). Acknowledge other factors (trial quality, true heterogeneity) that can cause funnel-plot asymmetry; report methods in detail and interpret cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe methods for additional analyses and pre-specify them (Item 16)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe methods of additional analyses (e.g., sensitivity or subgroup analyses, meta-regression), indicating which were pre-specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensitivity analyses explore robustness of findings to methodological choices or data changes (e.g., inclusion criteria, risk-of-bias results). Subgroup analyses examine if effects vary by study/participant characteristics. Meta-regression examines quantitative influence of study characteristics on effect size but has limitations and risk of over-interpretation. State rationale and pre-specification status for each analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study selection reporting and flow diagram (Item 17)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give numbers of studies screened, assessed for eligibility, and included in the review, with reasons for exclusions at each stage, ideally with a flow diagram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report total records identified from all sources (databases, hand searches, reference lists, citation indices, experts), numbers after duplicates removed, numbers excluded after screening, reports retrieved for detailed evaluation, potentially eligible reports not retrievable, retrieved reports that did not meet criteria with primary reasons for exclusion. Delineate sources of selected articles so readers can judge susceptibility to citation or publication bias. Prefer reporting number of studies (not just citations) and consider separate flow diagrams for important outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report study characteristics (Item 18)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each included study, present characteristics for which data were extracted (e.g., study size, PICOS, follow-up period) and provide the citation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present study-level characteristics typically as a table to ensure completeness and to indicate missing or unclear information. Include clinical characteristics, disease severity, intervention details (key elements for non-pharmacological interventions), timing of outcome measures, languages and geographic origins, and any unpublished sources identified from investigators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess and present risk of bias within studies (Item 19)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present data on risk of bias of each study and, if available, any outcome-level assessment, using a standard approach with defined criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reporting only summary statements (e.g., 'trials adequately concealed allocation'); instead explicitly report which studies had which methodological shortcomings and substantiate assessments with text from original studies where possible (e.g., Cochrane risk-of-bias tool). Present data in a table and provide narrative summary as helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present results of individual studies (Item 20)
rubrics_metrics.description: For all outcomes considered (benefits and harms), present, for each study: (a) simple summary data for each intervention group and (b) effect estimates and confidence intervals, ideally with a forest plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Binary outcomes: give frequencies with and without the event (e.g., 12/45), not just percentages. Continuous outcomes: provide mean, standard deviation, and sample size for each group. Time-to-event outcomes: report log hazard ratio and its standard error (or CI). Include group-specific summary data so readers can inspect event rates and detect extraction errors. Present numerical data, sample size, CI, and percentage weight with forest plots. Indicate which results were estimated or imputed and include unpublished data where applicable. Ensure harms outcomes are reported and avoid selective omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present syntheses of results and handle heterogeneity (Item 21)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the main results of the review; if meta-analyses are done, include for each confidence intervals and measures of consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an orderly presentation: initial narrative descriptions (study populations, design, conduct) to inform applicability and bias. If there is marked variation in study designs/participants/interventions/outcomes, consider qualitative synthesis rather than meta-analysis and justify. When heterogeneity is detected, explore possible reasons (e.g., subgroup differences), consider sensitivity analyses (e.g., excluding divergent trials), and report the impact on pooled estimates and heterogeneity measures (e.g., change in I2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting and addressing selective publication and outcome reporting bias (Box 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic reviews should consider bias from non-publication of studies and selective reporting of outcomes within published studies, as these can seriously threaten validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Missing studies are more likely when results are non-significant; missing outcomes occur when measured outcomes are not reported. Compare study protocols with published reports when available, use trial registries to identify missing studies, examine relations between effect size and sample size (precision) using funnel plots and tests for small-study bias, and interpret these analyses cautiously because other causes may explain patterns. Report evidence of selective reporting and its likely impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish counts (records, publications, studies) and note duplicate reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Be consistent in reporting counts (citations, records, publications, studies) and note duplicate or supplementary reports so readers understand the number of individual studies versus reports included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A flow diagram should depict studies included based on eligibility whether or not data were combined. Clarify when multiple reports correspond to one study and present counts of unique studies as most informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide study-level data to allow reproducibility and further analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish summary data from individual studies to enable reproduction and alternative analyses by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing study-level data allows readers to re-run analyses, assess the impact of excluding studies, perform subgroup analyses, detect data extraction errors (which are common), and examine consistency of standard deviations across studies to avoid confusions (e.g., SD vs SE). If too much information for a print report, include key outcomes in main report and provide additional data as web appendix.
